title: Linux.Proxy.10_Incident_Response_Scenario_ed3
description: Investigate and respond to a Linux.Proxy.10 trojan compromise on a victim host.

levels.title: Introduction
levels.content: The victim host in your network has been compromised by the Linux.Proxy.10 trojan, which is designed to run a SOCKS5 proxy server on the infected device. This trojan is used by cybercriminals to maintain anonymity online. Your task is to investigate and respond to this incident.

levels.title: Get Access
levels.cloud_content:
You have SSH access to the victim host with the following credentials:
- Hostname: victim
- IP Address: 192.168.60.10
- Username: cyrano
- Password: cyrano

To proceed, enter 'start' in the provided input field.
levels.local_content:
You have SSH access to the victim host with the following credentials:
- Hostname: victim
- IP Address: 192.168.60.10
- Username: cyrano
- Password: cyrano

To proceed, enter 'start' in the provided input field.

Local sandbox access is not required for this scenario.

levels.title: Investigate Suspicious Services
levels.content: Investigate the victim host for any unauthorized or suspicious services running on the system. Enumerate running services and distinguish legitimate services from trojan-related services. Look specifically for systemd timers that might be related to the malware. The answer is the name of a systemd timer.
levels.solution: Check the status of all services and look for any that appear unusual or out of place. Use commands like `systemctl list-units --type=service` to list all services and `systemctl status <service_name>` to check the status of specific services. Pay special attention to systemd timers that might be related to the malware.

hints.title: First hint title
hints.content: Check the status of all services and look for any that appear unusual or out of place.

hints.title: Second hint title
hints.content: Use commands like `systemctl list-units --type=service` to list all services and `systemctl status <service_name>` to check the status of specific services.

hints.title: Third hint title
hints.content: Look for services that are not part of the standard system installation or have unusual names. Pay special attention to systemd timers that might be related to the malware.

levels.title: Identify Scheduled Task or Timer
levels.content: Determine whether a scheduled task or timer is responsible for automatically executing the malware on the victim host. Identify scheduled execution persistence mechanisms (e.g., cron, systemd timers, Windows Scheduled Tasks). Look specifically for the network-diagnostics.timer that might be related to the malware. The answer is the name of a systemd timer.
levels.solution: Examine the systemd timers and services to find any that might be related to the malware. Use commands like `systemctl list-timers` to list all timers and `systemctl status <timer_name>` to check the status of specific timers. Pay special attention to the network-diagnostics.timer that might be related to the malware.

hints.title: First hint title
hints.content: Examine the systemd timers and services to find any that might be related to the malware.

hints.title: Second hint title
hints.content: Use commands like `systemctl list-timers` to list all timers and `systemctl status <timer_name>` to check the status of specific timers.

hints.title: Third hint title
hints.content: Look for timers that trigger scripts or executables in unusual locations. Pay special attention to the network-diagnostics.timer that might be related to the malware.

levels.title: Locate Malware Files
levels.content: Locate files installed by the malware on the compromised host. Correlate suspicious activity with files introduced by the trojan. Look specifically for the /var/lib/.netd/install.log file that might be related to the malware. The answer is a file path.
levels.solution: Search for hidden directories and files that might contain malware components or collected data. Use commands like `find / -type d -name '.*' 2>/dev/null` to find hidden directories and `find / -type f -name '.*' 2>/dev/null` to find hidden files. Pay special attention to the /var/lib/.netd/install.log file that might be related to the malware.

hints.title: Third hint title
hints.content: Pay special attention to files in directories like /var/lib/ or /tmp/ that might have been created recently. Look specifically for the /var/lib/.netd/install.log file that might be related to the malware.
